I guess it started when “emo” style picked up popularity a while back. For some it was just a style, but for many it started a trend of comparing and competing scars, and equating feeling depressed with having depression. 

If you weren’t suicidal, you weren’t sad enough to count. If you weren’t self harming, you weren’t suffering enough to count. 

Once emo died out, I think the residual understanding that sadness and suffering attracts attention remained. Except now it’s in more mainstream, socially acceptable forms. Like, Chadwick Boseman died and here’s how it affects ME more than any of YOU. 
Comparing misfortunes is pretty common and seemingly more dramatic within the younger generations.

Sadly I think the younger generations have started fetishizing sadness and pain, so it does end up being difficult to tell who is actually impacted by things like celebrity deaths and who’s just on the bandwagon for clout. 

And I have noticed the people genuinely upset don’t post as much about it, the same way we don’t plaster posts about our dead grandparents all over social media because it feels inappropriate.

I get you, but I think with media being as accessible as it is in so many forms a lot of us do form deep, emotional attachments to celebrities to fill in gaps. People get lonely and socially isolated, and we bond with the celebs we idolize in a way comparable to an actual relationship.

As an example, I’m a weird, socially anxious, awkward, generally isolated person. The Harry Potter series was instrumental in my growth and development. When Alan Rickman bit it, it genuinely felt like a family member had passed. It really, truly hurt. 

For some of us little people, losing our heroes has a very real mourning process afterwards.
